name: Per-token detokenisation, EOS/stop-string detection, and the host work they put on the critical path
arithmetic_intensity: This class has no bytes-per-flop at all: it is host-side text processing that runs once per generated token, on the API server's critical path, outside the model's arithmetic. Two costs, and they scale differently. (1) PER-TOKEN DETOKENISATION: the new token id is turned into text. In the shipped vLLM path this is a lookup into the tokenizer's DecodeStream plus the native incremental decode of that one piece - a vocab-table lookup (llama.cpp's token_to_piece consults a cache_token_to_piece table) and a UTF-8 decode of the piece. The published failure mode shows what the lookup can cost when it is written badly: detokenize_incrementally evaluated len(tokenizer) on EVERY generated token to range-check the id, and DeepseekV32Tokenizer.__len__ returned vocab_size + len(self.get_added_vocab()), where get_added_vocab() called into the native tokenizer each time - so a 1-token range check triggered a native added-vocab map rebuild/lookup (visible as BTreeMap::insert) on the GIL-holding main thread, once per token. (2) STOP-STRING DETECTION: per step, per stop string, a substring search over the newly generated characters. vLLM's check_stop_strings does output_text.find(stop_str, 1 - new_char_count - len(stop_str)) once PER STOP STRING, and it works because stop_buffer_length = max(len(s) for s in stop) - 1 characters are deliberately held back from the stream - so the scan window is bounded by new chars plus stop length, not by output length. That hold-back is the price of correctness at token boundaries: a stop string can straddle any token, so the engine must withhold up to max_stop_len - 1 characters and cannot emit them until it knows they are not part of a match. So the per-step cost is O(num_stop_strings x (new_chars + max_stop_len)) of host substring search plus O(bytes emitted) of holding, and it does NOT grow with sequence length - the one class in this family with a bounded per-step cost, provided the engine does the bounded-window search.
scales_with: num_generated_tokens (both costs run once per token, on the host, inside the streaming path)
num_stop_strings (one substring search per stop string per step)
max_stop_string_length (the hold-back is max(len(s)) - 1 characters, so a long stop string withholds a long tail of the stream and widens every scan window)
include_stop_str_in_output (when false, the hold-back applies and stop_buffer_length > 0; when true it is 0 and the scan window shrinks to the new characters)
vocab_size (only through the tokenizer's added-vocab / piece-cache lookup cost - a 152064-vocab tokenizer does more per-token lookup work than a 32000 one)
bytes emitted per token (a byte-level BPE token can decode to several characters, widening the stop-string scan window)
number of concurrent streams on one event loop (the per-token work is serialised on the GIL/loop, so it multiplies with concurrency rather than amortising)
byte-fallback / partial-UTF-8 handling (an incomplete trailing codepoint must be held, so some steps emit nothing at all)
workarounds: Bound the initial DecodeStream priming - vLLM primed with the ENTIRE prompt, costing ~0.5-1.5 us/token of native prefill (~3 ms at 5K ids, ~9 ms at 15K, ~12 ms at 20K, tokenizers 0.22.2); priming with only the last 32 prompt ids costs ~7 us once per request
Cache anything the per-token lookup recomputes - the added-vocab dict and its size prefetched once at tokenizer init, which is the entire fix for the DeepSeek-V3.2 starvation

Do the bounded-window stop-string search, never a full-output search: scan only the new characters plus the hold-back, as vLLM's check_stop_strings does with find(stop_str, 1 - new_char_count - stop_string_len)

Prefilter by token id before doing text work: a step whose delta ids contain none of the precomputed ids whose text could supply a marker's final character cannot have completed the marker, answered in O(len(delta)) with no decoding

Run detokenisation off the model thread or in a Rust/native extension - the shipped symptom is that a per-token native call on the GIL-holding main thread starves the event loop and hangs even /health
Skip detokenisation entirely where the client does not need text (a tokenizer=None path exists in vLLM, returning an IncrementalDetokenizer that decodes nothing)
Bound the number of stop strings, and prefer stop TOKEN ids over stop strings where the sentinel can be expressed as a token
notes: CLASSIFICATION ARGUMENT, and the enum gap this record exists to document. The schema's flop class enum has prefill_attention | decode_gemm | decode_attention | moe_routing | moe_experts | norm_softmax | sampling | embedding | speculative_draft | speculative_verify | kv_transfer | quantization_overhead | custom_kernel. There is no detokenisation class, and detokenisation is not sampling: sampling turns a logit tensor into a token id, detokenisation turns a token id into text, and they sit on opposite ends of the step with a host round trip between them. It is also not norm_softmax (no tensor), not embedding (no lookup into an embedding matrix), and not custom_kernel in the launch_overhead sense used by custom-kernel-launch-overhead (which is per KERNEL LAUNCH; this is per TOKEN of host text processing). REQUESTED ENUM ADDITION for the schema owner: add class 'detokenization' (and, if the taxonomy wants to name the second cost separately, 'stop_detection'). Recorded under 'sampling' as the nearest existing value - it is the same 'post-logit, per-token, host-side, batch-invariant-per-sequence' neighbourhood - but a reader querying class=sampling to find 'what happens after the token is chosen' will get the wrong answer. bound_by 'launch_overhead' is the closest existing value and is defensible: the cost is CPU-side, per-step, un-overlappable because the next step's streaming output depends on this one, and independent of how much GPU work the step contains. A cleaner value would be 'host' or 'cpu'. DESIGN CONSEQUENCE, the part that matters operationally: this class is invisible in every tok/s benchmark and dominant in every latency benchmark, because it is measured in the API server, not the engine. The published DeepSeek-V3.2 report is the sharp form: model unchanged, GPU unchanged, throughput unchanged on paper, and the server is unhealthy because /health hangs - the CPU cannot service HTTP because the decode loop's per-token detokenisation owns the main thread. The second published form (the bounded-tail priming fix) is the TTFT form: ~12 ms of native detokenisation prefill at a 20K-token prompt lands verbatim in that request's streaming TTFT AND head-of-line blocks the SSE deltas of every other stream on the same loop, i.e. it is a p99 contamination mechanism, not just a latency cost. The PR notes the cost hits hardest exactly where GPU-side TTFT is otherwise best - long warm-prefix prompts (agents, RAG) served with prefix caching. THE THIRD FORM is the worst, and it is a quadratic: a reasoning-end predicate that re-detokenises the whole sequence every step for every running request decayed a production structured-output deployment from 260 to 170 tok/s at concurrency 50, with ~4.9 ms per decode step in that one predicate at 16k reasoning lengths, the GPU drawing ~150 W of a 300 W limit and EngineCore pinned below one CPU core. The lesson generalises: the failure mode of every host-side per-token predicate is O(sequence length) work per step, i.e. quadratic decode, and it looks like a GPU utilisation collapse. ENGINE-AUTHOR CHECKLIST this implies, each item traceable to a published fix: (a) nothing in the per-token path may depend on the full prompt or the full output - bound it to a tail (32 ids) or to the delta; (b) nothing may call into the native tokenizer in a way that rebuilds a vocab-sized structure; (c) any per-step predicate must be O(delta), prefilterable by token id; (d) the stop-string scan must be windowed, with a deliberate hold-back sized max_stop_len - 1 and no full-text rescan. CAVEAT: all three published cases are single-engine (vLLM) reports with the fix verified as 'CPU utilisation returned to normal' rather than as a published tok/s delta, so the magnitudes are indicative and the mechanisms are the durable claim. No measured per-token detokenisation microsecond count is available in this repo; where a doc needs one it must say 'no record' rather than quote the 0.5-1.5 us/token priming figure, which is a different operation (full-prompt prime, not incremental detokenisation).
